howto.name: How to place one AI product against all three regimes

steps.name: Fix the role
steps.text: Decide whether you are a provider or a deployer under the EU Act, which existing US laws already reach your use, and whether the service is offered to the public in China.

steps.name: Classify once, map three ways
steps.text: Take the EU risk tier as the anchor, then map it to the US state laws' consequential decision categories and to China's service types.

steps.name: List the pre-launch gates
steps.text: Conformity assessment and EU database registration; state impact assessments where required; CAC filing and security assessment in China.

steps.name: Write the disclosures
steps.text: Article 50 notices and marks, US adverse action and hiring notices, China's explicit and implicit content labels.

steps.name: Price the downside
steps.text: Turnover-based fines in the EU, per-violation and per-day penalties in Texas, and suspension or removal in China, which is the penalty that ends a business.

short: The EU AI Act, the United States' federal and state patchwork, and China's service-by-service measures, compared on who is regulated, risk classification, pre-launch duties, disclosure, enforcement and maximum penalty, each cited to the text.
title: EU, US and China Compared
subtitle: The three largest AI regimes on the same six questions
body_html:
On this page

  • Who is regulated
  • How risk is classified
  • What must happen before launch
  • What must be disclosed
  • Who enforces
  • The maximum penalty
  • What the table hides
  • Sources

The three largest AI regimes answer the same six questions in very different ways. The European Union has one horizontal statute with a risk ladder and fines scaled to global turnover. The United States has no federal AI statute; it regulates through existing agency powers, executive orders and a growing set of state laws, which the site tracks state by state. China regulates by instrument: a separate set of measures for each kind of service, with filing and labelling duties enforced by the Cyberspace Administration. Each answer below is cited to the governing text and links to the site's fuller page on it.

Who is regulated

QuestionEuropean UnionUnited StatesChina
InstrumentRegulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, in force 1 August 2024, amended by the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744No federal AI statute. Executive Order 14179 (January 2025) and the July 2025 AI Action Plan set federal policy; existing laws (FTC Act, ECOA, FCRA, Title VII, HIPAA) apply to AI as to anything else; state statutes such as Texas HB 149 and the California laws add dutiesInterim Measures for Generative AI Services (effective 15 August 2023); Deep Synthesis Provisions (10 January 2023); Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions (1 March 2022); AI-generated content labelling measures (1 September 2025); and the 2026 measures on intelligent agents and anthropomorphic services
Who is coveredProviders who place an AI system or general purpose model on the EU market, and deployers who use one, wherever they are established, if the output is used in the EU (Article 2)Whoever an existing law already reaches: employers, lenders, insurers, health providers, government contractors. State laws name developers and deployers; Texas HB 149 covers any person doing business in Texas or producing a product used by TexansProviders of services offered to the public in China, including foreign providers; the generative AI measures exclude organisations that develop and use models internally without offering them to the public (Article 2)

How risk is classified

European UnionUnited StatesChina
SchemeFour tiers: prohibited practices (Article 5), high risk (Article 6 and Annex III, plus products under Annex I), limited risk with transparency duties (Article 50), minimal risk. General purpose models sit on a separate track, with extra duties above a systemic risk threshold (Articles 51 to 55)No federal classification. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary. State laws borrow the EU's high-risk idea for consequential decisions in employment, credit, housing, health and education; Colorado's law did so and was repealed before taking effect, Texas HB 149 does not use a risk tierBy service type, not by risk score: a service is regulated by which measures it falls under. Public-facing services with public opinion attributes or social mobilisation capacity carry the heaviest duties, a security assessment and filing

What must happen before launch

European UnionUnited StatesChina
Assessment or registrationHigh-risk systems need a conformity assessment, technical documentation, a risk and quality management system, and registration in the EU database before being placed on the market (Articles 9 to 17, 43, 49). Under the Digital Omnibus, stand-alone Annex III high-risk duties apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product duties from 2 August 2028Nothing federal before launch. State laws require impact assessments for high-risk uses in some places; the Texas act requires disclosure to consumers and bans specific practices rather than pre-launch assessment. Federal procurement rules (OMB M-25-21) govern what agencies may buyAlgorithm filing with the CAC within ten working days for recommendation and deep synthesis services; a security assessment before launch for generative services with public opinion attributes; model and training data lawfulness duties on the provider (Generative AI Measures Articles 7, 17)

What must be disclosed

European UnionUnited StatesChina
To users and the publicArticle 50, applying from 2 August 2026: tell people when they interact with an AI system, mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable way, label deepfakes, and disclose AI-generated text on matters of public interest. Providers of general purpose models must publish a training content summary (Article 53)Sector by sector. Adverse action notices under ECOA and FCRA when AI decides credit; NYC Local Law 144 bias audits and notices for hiring tools; Texas HB 149 disclosure when a consumer interacts with AI in health care and by government; California's SB 53 transparency duties on frontier developers; FTC action against deceptive AI claimsExplicit and implicit labels on all AI-generated content under the 2025 labelling measures; service agreements and complaint channels; the anthropomorphic services measures of 2026 add duties on companion-style products

Who enforces

European UnionUnited StatesChina
AuthorityNational market surveillance authorities in each member state; the European AI Office for general purpose models; the AI Board coordinating (Articles 64 to 70)The FTC, CFPB, EEOC, HHS OCR and SEC under their own statutes; state attorneys general under state AI and consumer protection laws; private lawsuits, which the site tracks in its lawsuit tracker. A December 2025 executive order directed a federal task force to challenge state AI lawsThe Cyberspace Administration of China, with the NDRC, MIIT, public security and market regulators, under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law and Personal Information Protection Law

The maximum penalty

European UnionUnited StatesChina
Ceiling as the text states itUp to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; EUR 15 million or 3 percent for most other breaches; EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent for supplying incorrect information (Article 99)Depends on the statute. Texas HB 149: civil penalties of USD 10,000 to 12,000 per curable violation, 80,000 to 200,000 per uncurable violation, and 2,000 to 40,000 per day for continuing violations, after a 60-day cure period. Colorado's repealed act carried the state's consumer protection penalty of up to USD 20,000 per violation. Federal agency penalties follow their own statutesThe AI measures themselves impose rectification orders, suspension and removal of a service; monetary penalties come from the underlying laws, with the Personal Information Protection Law reaching RMB 50 million or 5 percent of the prior year's turnover for serious breaches

What the table hides

Three things a table cannot show. First, the EU's dates moved: the Digital Omnibus deferred the stand-alone high-risk obligations by sixteen months, and the site's EU AI Act page carries the current schedule. Second, the United States is not one regime but fifty-one, and a company selling nationally meets the strictest state it operates in; the enacted laws page lists every state statute that has passed, with a reading of each. Third, China's rules are enforced through filing and licensing as much as through fines, so the operative question there is whether a service was permitted to launch at all, which the China AI regulation page and its CAC filings page explain.

Sources

  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 2, 5, 6, 9 to 17, 43, 49 to 55, 64 to 70, 99; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus.
  • Texas HB 149, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, 2025, penalties section.
  • Colorado SB 24-205 and its repeal by SB 26-189, 2026.
  • Executive Order 14179, Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, January 2025; America's AI Action Plan, July 2025; the December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI.
  • Cyberspace Administration of China: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services, 2023; Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services, 2022; Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendation, 2021; Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Synthetic Content, 2025; Personal Information Protection Law, Article 66.
